query: The Last Call Everyone else seems to have a letter. The registrar, who has seen this a hundred times, pins a short list beside her window: posts still open for this year's graduates. "Some people find their work late," she says. "Some people find it here. Some people find it in a fortnight's time, in their mother's kitchen. Choose." Go back to where you worked You knock on a door you know. The person behind it remembers you, and remembers your work better than you do. "We'd been wondering when you'd ask," they say, and write your name on a list that matters. You knock on a door you know. They remember you warmly, and they've filled the post, last week, with someone who asked first. They wish you luck and mean it. Take the registrar's list You put your name to the first post on the list: a junior clerk's desk, stamps and ledgers, a window that looks at a wall. It isn't a dream. It is a start date, and today that feels like a great deal. Write to the post you really want You write the letter you'd been too proud to write at the fair, and send it before you can tear it up. A reply comes by the next owl: come and see us. You go. They say yes. You write the letter you'd been too proud to write at the fair. The reply is kind and short, and the post went in the autumn to someone who wrote then. Leave it until after graduation You thank the registrar and walk away from the window. The world will still be there in a fortnight. So, she says to your back, will her list.

A thin letter. You are "a strong candidate" and on "a short list", and they "hope to write again". It's not a no. It's not anything.
